dialogues.title: Dialogue 1
dialogues.setting: Mr. Wong is a stranger in town and asks a local person the way

lines.speaker: Wong
lines.zh: 我要搭飞机返英国，请问去飞机场要搭几多号巴士呀？
lines.jp: ngo5 jiu3 daap3 fei1 gei1 faan1 jing1 gwok3, cing2 man6 heoi3 fei1 gei1 coeng4 jiu3 daap3 gei2 do1 hou6 baa1 si2 aa3?
lines.en: I need to take a flight to Britain, which bus should I take to the airport?

lines.speaker: Local
lines.zh: 呢处冇巴士去飞机场啵。你要先由呢处搭小巴一直去，过三个街口到大马路，喺巴士站你要落小巴，再转搭十五号巴士去飞机场喇。

dialogues.title: Dialogue 2
dialogues.setting: Mr. Wong visits Britain and is met by his friend Mr. Chan

grammar.title: cing2 man6: please may I ask…?
grammar.summary: cing2 man6 is the polite way to begin a question to a stranger or to someone of higher status.
grammar.body: cing2 man6, a combination of please and ask, is the polite way to begin a question to a stranger and is very useful therefore when asking directions. It is also the respectful way to begin a question to someone of higher status than yourself.

examples.jp: cing2 man6

grammar.title: To travel by
grammar.summary: co5 (to sit) can be used like daap3 to mean to travel by, but daap3 cannot be used to mean to sit.
grammar.body:
In unit 3 we were introduced to daap3 to travel by and in the same unit we met co5 to sit. Co5 can actually be used like daap3 to mean to travel by as well, probably because when you take transport you sit on it (if you're lucky!).
Beware, however: you cannot do the opposite and get away with making daap3 mean to sit

examples.jp: daap3 baa1 si2
co5 baa1 si2

grammar.title: First this, then that
grammar.summary: The adverbs first and then are sin1 and zoi3; they come before verbs.
grammar.body: The adverbs first and then are sin1 and zoi3. Being adverbs they come before verbs.

examples.jp: keoi5 sin1 heoi3 gei1 coeng4 zoi3 co5 baa1 si6 faan1 nguk1 kei5
examples.en: He's going first to the airport and then taking the bus home

grammar.title: More shortcuts
grammar.summary: The full word for underground railway, dei6 haa6 tit3 lou6, is usually reduced to dei6 tit3.
grammar.body:
The full formal word for an underground railway dei6 haa6 tit3 lou6 is far too much of a mouthful for most people, who reduce it to dei6 tit3.
The underground railway in Hong Kong, dei6 tit3, is known in English as the MTR, short for Mass Transit Railway.
Since 1998 it has been possible to interchange to the very fast Airport Express Line between Chek Lap Kok International Airport and Central district (zung1 waan4) next to the famous Star Ferry Pier (Tin1 sing1 maa5 tau4).

examples.jp: dei6 haa6 tit3 lou6
dei6 tit3
zung1 waan4
tin1 sing1 maa5 tau4

grammar.title: lou5
grammar.summary: lou5 (elderly) is used only for people and animals; lou5 + surname is a familiar address to a man, and the surname changes to a mid rising tone.
grammar.body:
lou5 means elderly, aged and is used only for people and animals (that is you would not describe a building or a book as lou5). It is often used with the surname as a familiar or affectionate term of address to a man (rarely to a woman).
Note that when this is done the tone of the surname is changed to a mid rising tone from the original low falling tone.

examples.jp: lou5 wong2…
wong4
lou5 wong2
can4
lou5 can2

grammar.title: Ordinal numbers
grammar.summary: Ordinals are formed with dai6 before the cardinal number (dai6 ji6, not loeng5); dai6 ji6 can also mean the next, the other, the others.
grammar.body:
We met the cardinal numbers (one, two, three, four, etc.) in Unit 2. The ordinal numbers (the first, the second, the third, the fourth, etc.) are formed by putting dai6 in front of the cardinal number.
You will remember from Unit 2 that the number two obeys different rules. So that becomes ji6 becomes loeng5 in front of classifiers. Note that with ordinal numbers there is no such exception.
dai6 ji6 as well as the second can quite logically extend to mean the next.
It can also logically extend to mean the other.
But you need to stretch your mind a little further to take in the notion that dai6 ji6 can mean the others.

grammar.title: To tell
grammar.summary: When tell means tell someone about something, use waa6 … teng1.
grammar.body: Tell has various meanings in English and they are not all translated by the same word in Cantonese. When tell means tell someone about something you can use waa6

examples.jp: keoi5 waa6 ngo5 teng1 keoi5 m4 sik1 zaa1 ce1

grammar.title: Directions
grammar.summary: The four directions are dung1, naam4, sai1, bak1; intermediate directions are the opposite way round from English (Eastnorth for Northeast).
grammar.body: Cantonese lists the four directions in the order given here, though English speakers normally start with north. The intermediate directions are straightforward provided you remember that they are always the opposite way round from English, i.e. Cantonese says Eastnorth where English says Northeast.

grammar.title: Movement: hoeng3, jau4, dou3, ging1, lei4
grammar.summary: hoeng3 = towards; jau4 = starting point (from), with dou3 for the end point; ging1 = via; lei4 = distance from a location. Prepositional phrases come before the verb.
grammar.body:
Movement towards a point in space may be expressed by hoeng3.
To express a starting point in time or space, jau4 is used as follows.
Prepositional phrase comes before the verb
jau4 is also used together with dou3 indicating the end point of a journey in time or space.
Ging1 'via' introduces an intermediate step between the starting point and end point.
Lei4 is used to indicate distance from a location.
A verb is not needed here

grammar.title: Another verb ending: -jyun4 finished
grammar.summary: -jyun4 as a verb ending shows that the action of the verb is all over with.
grammar.body: jyun4 means the end or to finish. It is used as a verb ending to show that the action of the verb is all over with.

examples.jp: sik6 jyun4
caam1 gun1 jyun4

grammar.title: 'Time when'
grammar.summary: Time-when expressions come before the verb of the main statement; after-clauses end with zi1 hau6.
grammar.body:
Time expression which begin with after are translated with zi1 hau6 in Cantonese, but zi1 hau6 is placed at the end of the time expression not at the beginning.
In English the after you'd gone could come at the end of the sentence (She told me you don't like prawns after you'd gone), but with expressions which pinpoint the time when something happens Cantonese likes to have the information before the verb of the main statement is given, so you do not have the option of putting nei5 zau2 zo2 zi1 hau6 at the end.
Other time when expressions you have met so far, such as gam1 jat6 today and lai5 baai3 ng5 Friday, as well as the many you haven't yet met (at 6 o'clock; in May last year; when I got there; before he had breakfast; in 1492 AD), all obey the same rule.

examples.jp: nei5 zau2 zo2 zi1 hau6, keoi5 waa6 ngo5 teng1 nei5 m4 zung1 ji3 sik6 haa1
examples.en: After you'd gone she told me you don't like prawns

examples.jp: lai5 baai3 jat6 nei5 heoi3 m4 heoi3 aa1?
ngo5 gam1 jat6 soeng2 heoi3 jau4 seoi2
examples.en: I'd like to go swimming today

grammar.title: Can, able to
grammar.summary: sik1 = have learned how to; ho2 ji5 = permission / absence of obstacles; verb ending -dak1 is an all-purpose can that attaches directly to a verb.
grammar.body:
You met sik1 in Unit 4 and in this unit comes ho2 ji5: both mean can, able to. They are not usually interchangeable. sik1 really means to have learned how to and implies that you are able to do something because you have acquired the skill to do it (speak a foreign language, ride a bicycle, eat with chopsticks, etc.). ho2 ji5 operates in the realm of permission (may) and absence of obstacles to doing something.
Another way to say can, be able is by using the verb ending -dak1. This is actually the same word that we met in Unit 5, but in this use it must go directly onto a verb.
With -dak1 there is no guidance as to whether he can drive because he knows how to, because his father says he may, because he has his full physical powers or because there is a car available, so it is a good all-purpose way of saying can. Do remember though that -dak1 can only be put onto a verb, not onto any other part of speech.

examples.jp: nei5 sik1 m4 sik1 zaa1 ce1 aa3?
examples.en: Can you drive (do you know how to drive)?

examples.jp: nei5 ho2 ji5 m4 ho2 ji5 zaa1 ce1 aa3?
examples.en: Can you drive (Have you got a license? Is the car available?)

examples.jp: ngo5 m4 heoi3 dak1
keoi5 zaa1 dak1 ce1

grammar.title: 'Time how long'
grammar.summary: Time expressions showing how long something goes for come after the main verb.
grammar.body: Time expressions which show how long something goes for (as opposed to the time when something happens) come after the main verb in Cantonese.

examples.jp: daap3 gam3 noi6 ce1
examples.en: Traveling in a car for so long

examples.jp: ngo5 dei6 hai2 hoeng1 gong2 zyu6 loeng5 go3 lai5 baai3
examples.en: We are staying in Hong Kong for two weeks

examples.jp: keoi5 co5 zo2 ng5 go3 zung1 tau4 fei1 gei1
examples.en: He was on the plane for five hours

grammar.title: Yet another verb ending: -gwo3 to have had the experience
grammar.summary: -gwo3 shows the verb has been experienced at some time; -zo2 shows completion at a particular point in time.
grammar.body:
gwo3 literally means to go past, as you saw earlier in this unit. As a verb ending -gwo3 shows that the verb has been experienced at some time.
-zo2, as we saw in Unit 4, shows that an action has been completed at a particular point in time; -gwo3 shows the an action has at some time or other occurred.

examples.en: I have had prawns (I have experienced eating prawns)

examples.jp: keoi5 heoi3 zo2 hoeng1 gong2
keoi5 heoi3 gwo3 hoeng1 gong2
examples.en: He has been to Hong Kong

examples.jp: nei5 tai2 gwo3 ji1 saang1 maa1?
examples.en: Have you ever been to the doctor's?

grammar.title: Making comparison
grammar.summary: gwo3 = 'more (adjective) than (noun)' with English-like word order; when no 'than' is expressed, di1 is used instead.
grammar.body:
Where two things are explicitly being compared, gwo3 is used to mean 'more (adjective) than (noun)'. The word order is similar to English.
If the object of comparison is not expressed (i.e. there is no 'than…'), di1 is used instead.
Di1 literally means 'a little' but here serves largely to indicate a difference between the two items with respect to some property

examples.jp: Jenny sai3 gwo3 ngo5
baat3 lau2 hou2 gwo3 ji6 lau2
examples.en: The eighth floor is better than the second floor

examples.jp: ni1 deoi3 gwai3 gwo3 go2 deoi3
examples.en: This pair is more expensive than that one

examples.jp: Jenny sai3 di1
baat3 lau2 hou2 di1
ni1 deoi3 gwai3 di1

grammar.title: Modifying comparisons
grammar.summary: Adverbs of degree (hou2 do1, siu2 siu2, gei2 pui5) go at the end of a gwo3 comparison, and replace di1; zung6 'even' comes before the adjective.
grammar.body:
Both kinds of comparison can be modified by adverbs of degree such as hou2 do1 'much' and siu2 siu2 'a little' as follows:
(i) in comparison with gwo3, the adverb of degree is simply added at the end of the construction.
(ii) in comparisons where di1 would normally be used, a degree word such as hou2 do1 'a lot' replaces di1.
The reason for this is that di1 literally means 'a bit', so that to combine it with an adverb like hou2 do1 'a lot' would be a contradiction in terms. This shows that di1 as in leng3 di1 is not really equivalent to the suffix -er in English 'prettier'
Zung6 'even' can be applied to both the gwo3 and di1 constructions, but comes before the adjective.
di1 can be omitted here since the presence of zung6 implies that a comparison is being made

examples.jp: nei5 lek1 gwo3 keoi5 hou2 do1
keoi5 gou1 gwo3 nei5 siu2 siu2
examples.en: She's a little taller than you

examples.jp: ngo5 daai6 gwo3 keoi5 jat1 nin4
examples.en: I'm a year older than her

examples.jp: ni1 go3 gwai3 siu2 siu2
examples.en: This one is a little more expensive (from ni1 go3 gwai3 di1)

examples.jp: ni1 go3 cung5 gei2 pui5
examples.en: This one is several times heavier (from ni1 go3 cung5 di1)

examples.jp: gam1 ci3 zung6 hou2 gwo3 soeng6 ci3

grammar.title: Alternative forms of comparison: bei2
grammar.summary: With bei2, the object of comparison comes before the adjective; a modifying phrase still comes after the adjective.
grammar.body:
The word order is quite different since bei2 and the object of comparison come before the adjective.
A modifying phrase comes after the adjective, as with gwo3.

grammar.title: Bei2 vs. gwo3
grammar.summary: bei2 is more formal and allows change-of-state comparisons; gwo3 can also be omitted if a phrase showing the degree of difference is added.
grammar.body:
Bei2 is more formal than gwo3. The bei2 form allow some comparisons which would not be possible with gwo3, such as those expressing a change of state.
Yet another alternative is to omit gwo3 but add a phrase showing the degree of difference.

examples.lit: She compare last year got thinner

examples.lit: You compared last time improved

examples.lit: We fast him one step

grammar.title: Comparison with dimensional adjectives
grammar.summary: daai6 and sai3 are often used without gwo3 to mean 'older' and 'younger', with the degree phrase after the object.
grammar.body: This comparison is commonly found with daai6 and sai3, which are often used in this way to mean 'older' and 'younger' respectively.

examples.jp: nei5 go4 go1 daai6 nei5 gei2 do1 aa3?
examples.en: How much older is your brother than you?
examples.lit: Your brother big you how much?

examples.jp: keoi5 sai3 ngo5 jat1 nin4
examples.en: She's a year younger than me
examples.lit: She small me one year

grammar.title: Comparison of adverbs
grammar.summary: gwo3, di1 or bei2 are added to adverbial constructions with dak1; when the verb has an object, both verb and object are repeated.
grammar.body:
Comparison using gwo3, di1, or bei2 are added to adverbial constructions with dak1.
The main difficulty arises where the verb has an object and both are repeated.

examples.jp: keoi5 duk6 dak1 faai3 gwo3 ngo5
examples.en: He reads faster than I do
examples.lit: He read manner quicker than me

examples.jp: nei5 se2 dak1 leng3 di1
examples.lit: You write manner nicer

examples.jp: keoi5 dei6 bei2 ngo5 dei6 zou6 dak1 hou2
examples.en: They do it better than we do
examples.lit: They compare us do manner well

examples.jp: keoi5 tai2 zung1 man2 tai2 dak1 faai3 gwo3 ngo5
examples.en: He reads Chinese more quickly than I do
examples.lit: He reads Chinese reads manner quick than me

examples.jp: nei5 se2 zi6 se2 dak1 leng3 di1
examples.lit: You write characters write manner nicer

examples.jp: keoi5 dei6 zou6 saang1 ji3 bei2 ngo5 dei6 zou6 dak1 hou2
examples.en: They do business better than we do
examples.lit: They do business compare us do manner well

grammar.title: Superlatives
grammar.summary: Superlatives use zeoi3 (or colloquial zi3), attributively with ge3 or predicatively with hai6; the range of comparison is specified before the superlative.
grammar.body:
Expressed straightforwardly by zeoi3, or as a colloquial alternative by zi3.
These forms are typically used as follows:
(i) attributively with ge3
(ii) predicatively with hai6
The order is often reversed beginning with the superlative expression as the subject.
The range in which the comparison is to be made is specified before the superlative form.

exercises.title: Exercise 1
exercises.instructions: Insert the lettered elements into each sentence. Elements: A. daap3 ce1; B. sap6 ng5 hou6; C. sai3 gaai3 zeoi3 jau5 meng2 ge3; D. m4 heoi3 fei1 gei1 coeng4; E. gwo3 saam1 go3 gaai1 hau2 dou3 faa1 jyun4 dou6

items.prompt: gim3 kiu4 daai6 hok6 hai6 daai6 hok6 zi1 jat1
items.answer: gim3 kiu4 daai6 hok6 hai6 sai3 gaai3 zeoi3 jau5 meng2 ge3 daai6 hok6 zi1 jat1
items.answer_en: Cambridge University is one of the most famous universities in the world

items.prompt: jau4 leon4 deon1 heoi3 gim3 kiu4 daai6 hok6 caam1 gun1 jiu3 hoeng3 bak1 haang4
items.answer: jau4 leon4 deon1 daap3 ce1 heoi3 gim3 kiu4 daai6 hok6 caam1 gun1 jiu3 hoeng3 bak1 haang4
items.answer_en: To go by car from London to visit Cambridge University you have to head north

items.prompt: jau4 ni1 cyu3 daap3 baa1 si2 heoi3 fei1 gei1 coeng4 jiu3 gei2 do1 cin2 aa3?
items.answer: jau4 ni1 cyu3 daap3 sap6 ng5 hou6 baa1 si2 heoi3 fei1 gei1 coeng4 jiu3 gei2 do1 cin2 aa3?
items.answer_en: How much does it cost to take the No. 15 bus from here to the airport?

items.prompt: ni1 cyu3 ge3 dei6 haa6 tit3 lou6 zi2 heoi3 daai6 wui6 tong4
items.answer: ni1 cyu3 ge3 dei6 haa6 tit3 lou6 zi2 heoi3 daai6 wui6 tong4 m4 heoi3 fei1 gei1 coeng4
items.answer_en: The underground railway here only goes to the City Hall, not to the airport

items.prompt: nei5 jiu3 daap3 baa1 si2 heoi3 fei1 gei1 coeng4
items.answer: nei5 jiu3 gwo3 saam1 go3 gaai1 hau2 dou3 faa1 jyun4 dou6 daap3 baa1 si2 heoi3 fei1 gei1 coeng4
items.answer_en: You have to go past three junctions to Garden Road and take the bus to the airport

exercises.title: Exercise 2
exercises.instructions: Tell direction using Cantonese. Use the map: the airport (fei1 gei1 coeng4) and the City Hall (daai6 wui6 tong4) both lie on the same east-west road (airport to the west, City Hall to the east). From the City Hall junction a road runs south, crossing three streets, then turns east to the restaurant (zau2 lau4).

items.prompt: 张先生张太太请我食饭。唔该你话我听由飞机场点样去酒楼呀？ Zoeng1 sin1 saang1 Zoeng1 taai3 taai2 cing2 ngo5 sik6 faan6. m4 goi1 nei5 waa6 ngo5 teng1 jau4 fei1 gei1 coeng4 dim2 joeng2 heoi3 zau2 lau4 aa3?
items.answer_en: Mr. and Mrs. Cheung have invited me to dinner. Please tell me how to get from the airport to the restaurant
items.hint: Use jau4 … hoeng3 … haang4, gwo3 … go3 gaai1 hau2, dou3, zyun2 and the directions dung1 / naam4

exercises.title: Practice 1
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the following comparisons would use gwo3 or di1, and translate as much of the sentence as you can into Cantonese.

items.prompt: It's warmer today
items.answer: gam1 jat6 nyun5 di1
items.answer_en: di1 (no 'than')

items.prompt: She's happier now
items.answer_en: di1 (no 'than')

items.prompt: My friend is older than me
items.answer: ngo5 pang4 jau5 daai6 gwo3 ngo5
items.answer_en: gwo3 (explicit 'than')

items.prompt: She's much taller than before
items.answer: keoi5 gou1 gwo3 ji5 cin4 hou2 do1
items.answer_en: gwo3 (explicit 'than'), degree adverb at the end

items.prompt: It's slower this time
items.answer_en: di1 (no 'than')

items.prompt: This restaurant is cheaper than that one
items.answer: ni1 gaan1 zau2 lau4 peng4 gwo3 go2 gaan1
items.answer_en: gwo3 (explicit 'than')

items.answer_en: gwo3 (explicit 'than')

items.prompt: Your idea is better
items.answer: nei5 ge3 zyu2 ji3 hou2 di1

exercises.title: Practice 2
exercises.instructions: Make any meaningful comparison between the following.

items.prompt: Today (gam1 jat6) and yesterday (kam4 jat6)
Girls (neoi5 zai2) and boys (naam4 zai2)
Shirts (seot1 saam1) and ties (leng5 taai1)
Toronto (do1 leon4 do1) and London (leon4 deon1)
Chinese (zung1 man2) and English (jing1 man2)
Swimming (jau4 seoi2) and jogging (paau2 bou6)
Cantonese food (gwong2 dung1 coi3) and Chiu Chow food (ciu4 zau1 coi3)
Doing business (zou6 saang1 ji3) and teaching (gaau3 syu1)

exercises.title: Practice 3
exercises.instructions: Make the following comparisons more explicit using the adverb given in brackets.

items.prompt: gam1 nin2 dung3 gwo3 gau6 nin2 — This year is (much) colder than last year
items.answer: gam1 nin2 dung3 gwo3 gau6 nin2 hou2 do1

items.answer: nei5 di1 tau4 faat3 ji4 gaa1 dyun2 siu2 siu2
items.answer_en: Your hair is a little shorter now

items.prompt: hoeng1 gong2 gwai3 gwo3 ni1 dou6 — Hong Kong is (several times) more expensive than here
items.answer: hoeng1 gong2 gwai3 gwo3 ni1 dou6 gei2 pui5
items.answer_en: Hong Kong is several times more expensive than here

items.prompt: ngo5 gui6 gwo3 keoi5 — I'm (even) more tired than she is
items.answer: ngo5 zung6 gui6 gwo3 keoi5
items.answer_en: I'm even more tired than she is

items.prompt: sik6 faan6 peng4 gwo3 sik6 min6 — Eating rice is (even) cheaper than eating noodles
items.answer: sik6 faan6 zung6 peng4 gwo3 sik6 min6
items.answer_en: Eating rice is even cheaper than eating noodles

items.prompt: gam1 ci3 hok6 fai3 bei2 soeng6 ci3 gwai3 — This time the tuition is (a hundred dollars) more expensive than last time
items.answer: gam1 ci3 hok6 fai3 bei2 soeng6 ci3 gwai3 jat1 baak3 man1

items.hint: degree phrase after the adjective, as with gwo3 ('a hundred dollars' is not taught in this unit)

items.prompt: keoi5 gou1 gwo3 ngo5 — She is (three times) taller than me
items.answer: keoi5 gou1 gwo3 ngo5 saam1 pui5
items.answer_en: She is three times taller than me

notes.title: The MTR (dei6 tit3)
notes.body:
The underground railway in Hong Kong, dei6 tit3, is known in English as the MTR, short for Mass Transit Railway. The first section of it was opened in 1979, 43km were in service by 1989 and new extensions are constantly being added. It is air-conditioned throughout (including the tunnels), clean, fast and efficient and fares are low. Hong Kong people are noticeably proud of the system. The trains have no barriers between the coaches, so that you can stand at one end and look down the full length of the side of the train as it snakes its way through the tunnels. For speed of travel through crowded Hong Kong it cannot bettered.
Since 1998 it has been possible to interchange to the very fast Airport Express Line which shuttles at up to 135 kilometers an hour between the new Chek Lap Kok International Airport and the very heart of Hong Kong in Central district (zung1 waan4) next to the famous Star Ferry Pier (Tin1 sing1 maa5 tau4).
